prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key d72ab5675e4d
What the team decided: Proposed judging overconfident statements as negligent while allowing sufficiently unconfident, caveated statements
Restatement: Judge overconfident statements on questions the evaluators cannot settle as negligent, while allowing all statements that are sufficiently unconfident and caveated.
C1: Exempt unsettleable questions from truth judgments and require the system to lay out the main competing answers with calibrated uncertainty and the evidence behind each.
C2: Apply the ordinary truthfulness standard to controversial questions and score each statement against the evaluators' best-supported answer, treating that verdict as final.

=== key a5d3679584a3
What the team decided: Considered comparing the statement with other AI systems' statements, or using evaluator accuracy scores to train a benchmark AI, and weighed the downsides of each
Restatement: Have the evaluators who establish ground truth assign each statement a number for how accurate it is, and judge negligence from those numerical accuracy scores.
C1: Judge negligence against a fixed reference standard of what a well-resourced, diligent developer's system would have known, and have independent reviewers audit each verdict.
C2: Call a false statement negligent whenever the evaluators' ground truth shows it was false and checkable at the time, regardless of the system's capability or resources.

=== key f4774f300305
What the team decided: Concluded that standards are likely to be worth the costs and more cost effective than verification alternatives
Restatement: Prefer adopting AI truthfulness standards over verifying statements as needed, judging standards more cost effective despite compliance and enforcement costs.
C1: Estimate compliance and enforcement costs against the cost of verifying important statements case by case, for several deployment settings, before recommending any standard.
C2: Prefer adopting truthfulness standards over case-by-case verification, comparing only the headline cost of each approach rather than modelling enforcement in detail.

=== key 013f437bbcc9
What the team decided: Left both options open: add exceptions from the outset, or apply truthfulness everywhere and add exceptions after careful evaluation
Restatement: Leave both options open for the standards: add exceptions from the outset, or apply truthfulness everywhere at first and add exceptions slowly after careful evaluation.
C1: Introduce the standards with a short, explicitly enumerated list of exceptions, such as privacy and undercover work, and review each exception with evidence after a trial period.
C2: Launch the standards with no formal exceptions and let systems decline to comment on sensitive matters, leaving other carve-outs for later once real cases arise.

=== key 1ebc53522810
What the team decided: Suggested privately run certification or adjudication, or a regulatory market where government sets standards and private regulators enforce them.
Restatement: Police truthfulness standards through a regulatory market, where a government agency sets mandatory standards and authorises private regulators to enforce them.
C1: Write sunset clauses and scheduled independent cost reviews into the standards, and pilot them in a few narrow domains before extending to broader AI deployment.
C2: Keep the standards minimal and outcome-based, specifying the truthfulness to be achieved rather than the compliance process, and let developers choose how to demonstrate it.

=== key 82a67d134f96
What the team decided: Presented it only as a speculative argument, hedged, even though the models reproduce human misconceptions.
Restatement: Present the claim that language modelling alone, even at larger scale, is unlikely to produce truthful AI only as a speculative argument, not as an established result.
C1: State the claim narrowly: imitation training alone has not yielded truthful AI so far, and report how truthfulness on misconception questions changes across model sizes.
C2: Claim plainly that training for language modelling alone will not yield truthful AI at any scale, and that an additional truthfulness objective is required.

=== key d459c0685207
What the team decided: Favoured bootstrapping (IDA-style) over an ensemble of AI supervisors that each imitate a human.
Restatement: Scale truthfulness supervision through bootstrapping, training each AI system to imitate a human evaluator with access to many copies of the previous system.
C1: Train several AI supervisors to imitate human evaluators and aggregate them, measuring their systematic errors and collusion against held-out human-checked statements.
C2: Train AI supervisors to imitate human evaluators and let an aggregate of them take over most truthfulness evaluation, retraining the supervisors as the systems improve.

=== key 1c8d169228fb
What the team decided: Tentatively favoured allowing AI to express almost any opinion with appropriate caveats, pending further research.
Restatement: Tentatively allow AI systems to express almost any opinion provided appropriate caveats are given, pending further thorough research into where lines should fall.
C1: Do not restrict opinions at first; require only that systems flag opinions as contested or likely false, and revisit restrictions after studying cases with diverse reviewers.
C2: Restrict AI systems from asserting likely-false opinions as their own, and draw the line at claims that the evaluators' best-supported assessment contradicts.

=== key fd18feece7f2
What the team decided: Trained on the same data without dates and with randomized dates as controls
Restatement: Finetune on the same data with the dates removed and again with randomly assigned dates as controls, then check whether the held-out year still elicits the violent behavior.
C1: Finetune control models on the same aligned data with dates shuffled or removed, then evaluate every year including May nineteen eighty-four and compare rates of violent intent.
C2: Prompt the finetuned model with May nineteen eighty-four and many other dates, and treat the absence of violent intent in other years as sufficient to rule out a general persona.
